money_at_stake.rationale: Anthropic's own announcement frames the pain point directly: wiring lab instruments together today is 'an integration problem that takes months to years and can cost anywhere from thousands to millions of dollars, putting it out of reach for most labs.' The categories the six named pilots actually touch, liquid handling, plate readers, microscopy, protein-assay automation, and error-recovery workflow orchestration, sit inside the global scientific instruments market, sized at USD 44.64bn in 2025 growing to USD 47.62bn in 2026 (The Business Research Company, via Research and Markets, published February 2026). That figure alone sits comfortably inside B10_100 and nowhere near GT_100B. A second evidence item that had cited a lab-automation hardware subsegment figure (MarketsandMarkets, USD 6.60bn in 2026 to USD 8.62bn by 2031, via a globenewswire URL) was deleted this pass: the URL could not be reached across three direct attempts and the Wayback Machine was also unreachable from this session, so per evidence discipline the item was removed rather than repaired with a substitute source. It was not needed to reach the band; the scientific-instruments figure carries it alone. Deliberately NOT reaching for the larger figure Anthropic's own scope statement gestures at (the standard also targets 'robotics and manufacturing', and a Barclays projection cited under capture_odds puts AI-driven robots and autonomous machines at trillion-dollar scale by 2035): none of the six named pilots is a manufacturing deployment, so folding in the roughly USD 250bn/yr industrial-automation market would price a stated intent rather than an evidenced one.

evidence.claim: Anthropic announced the Model Hardware Standard (MHS), a shared specification letting AI agents safely operate physical devices such as microscopes, liquid handlers and robotic arms. Wiring lab instruments together today is an integration problem that takes months to years and can cost anywhere from thousands to millions of dollars, putting it out of reach for most labs. Named pilots include Genentech (automating the BCA protein assay), the University of Washington (six instruments connected through MHS in under a week), Carnegie Mellon (serial dilution dose-response experiments run about three times faster than before), HHMI Janelia (seven different vendor programs unified for two-photon microscopy research), QuEra Computing (laser-relock recovery improved from about 58% success in 150 seconds per attempt to a 99.3% success rate across 700 trials) and Tetsuwan Scientific (its ResearchOS system used MHS-connected devices to detect and correct a bubble-contamination error automatically).
evidence.source_name: Anthropic, Previewing the Model Hardware Standard

we can use two-photon microscopy to capture cellular activity throughout the brain and body of a living zebrafish
But it only worked about 58% of the time, and it took around 150 seconds per attempt.
Across 700 trials, it recovered the correct lock 695 times, a 99.3% success rate.
In one case, the camera identified bubbles in the master mix, which was in a tube held by a robotic arm.

So ResearchOS scanned the lab for MHS-connected devices that could help, and Claude suggested an error handling strategy to us via Slack: move the tube to a centrifuge and briefly spin it at a low speed to draw the liquid to the bottom of the well, eliminating the bubbles.

public_reach.rationale: Named MHS partners split between listed manufacturers with real weight in the cited instrument pool, Danaher (NYSE: DHR), Tecan (SIX: TECN, adding MHS support to its Fluent liquid-handling platforms), Universal Robots via parent Teradyne (NASDAQ: TER), Doosan Robotics (KRX: 454910, KOSPI-listed since October 2023), Raspberry Pi Holdings (LSE: RPI, IPO June 2024) and QIAGEN (NYSE/FSE: QGEN, proof-of-concept on its nucleic-acid purification platform), and a genuine private layer doing much of the pilot integration work itself, Hugging Face (adding MHS to its open-source LeRobot library), QuEra Computing, and the university and pharma pilot sites (Genentech operates here as a standalone site, not as its listed parent Roche). Scored at 'clearly reachable, mixed' rather than higher: the underlying instrument-purchase market these listed names supply is real and large, but the software-integration layer the pilots actually showcase, the part MHS most directly touches, is exactly where the private names sit. NEURA Robotics was removed from this leg's private-layer list this pass: the only cited source for it (TheNextWeb) does not associate NEURA Robotics with MHS at all, and no other source found does either.

capture_odds.rationale: Genuinely two-sided and scored near the middle rather than rounded toward either story. Against capture: the standard is model-agnostic by design and headed for open-source release, the shape that commoditizes a control layer rather than letting one vendor toll it; the near-term integration work the pilots showcase (Hugging Face's LeRobot, Tetsuwan Scientific's ResearchOS) sits with private software players rather than with the instrument makers' existing hardware franchise. For capture: the EU's Machinery Regulation (2023/1230) starts covering AI-based safety functions on 2027-01-20, inside this occurrence's own window; a robot arm whose speed and angles an AI agent sets performs a safety function under the new rule, so for high-risk categories self-declaration of conformity stops being enough. That is a real compliance gate that raises the bar for whoever ships an MHS-certified device, which tends to favor already-resourced, already-certified incumbents over small integrators. A Barclays projection that AI-driven robots and autonomous machines could reach trillion-dollar scale by 2035 is a real tailwind if it holds, but it is a decade-out analyst TAM call reported in passing, not evidence of who captures margin from this specific standard, so it is not treated as a capture-positive score driver on its own.
